summary: IPsec peers use IKE to negotiate which cryptographic algorithms to use. To keep implementations interoperable, this document gives requirements and guidance on which algorithms IKEv2 implementations must or should support, and it keeps pace with changes in cryptography.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people need to agree on a language before they can talk. This tells VPN software which languages everyone must know and which are best.

which diffie hellman group is mandatory in ikev2
subtitle: Which cryptographic algorithms IKEv2 implementations must, should and must not support, so VPN peers can always agree.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 peers negotiate algorithms using local policy, so two implementations might share none unless a common baseline is defined, and that baseline ages as cryptography advances.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists, for each IKEv2 transform type and for authentication, a requirement level such as MUST, SHOULD or MUST NOT, and explains each change from RFC 4307.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4307 and updates RFC 7296, and it is itself updated by RFC 9395.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: IKEv2 only, not IKEv1, AH or ESP

today: RFC 8247 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2017. It obsoletes RFC 4307, updates RFC 7296, and is updated by RFC 9395.

sections.title: Why Mandatory-to-Implement Algorithms
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol negotiates the parameters of an IPsec Security Association, including the encryption and authentication algorithms and the keys. IKE itself is also protected by cryptographic algorithms, which the two endpoints negotiate using IKE. Different implementations may negotiate different algorithms based on their own local policy, so a set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms is defined to keep them interoperable.

This document updates RFC 7296 and obsoletes RFC 4307. The selection of algorithms was removed from the main IKEv2 specification and placed in a separate document, because requirements need to change over time. It covers IKEv2 only; IKEv1 is out of scope, and it does not describe the algorithms for the AH or ESP protocols.

The document gives implementation recommendations, not advice on what a user should deploy. A user's own security policy decides which algorithms are actually used.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who builds VPN software needs to agree on a few shared tools so any two programs can work together. This document keeps that list up to date.

sections.title: Requirement Levels and How They Change
sections.content:
The tables use the RFC 2119 words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY, plus three extra terms. SHOULD+ means SHOULD, but the algorithm is likely to be promoted to MUST later. SHOULD- means SHOULD, but it may be deprecated to MAY later. MUST- means MUST, but it is expected to stop being a MUST in a future document, and it will probably remain at least SHOULD or SHOULD-.

Changes are meant to be gradual. Unless there are strong security reasons, an algorithm is expected to move from MUST to MUST- or SHOULD, instead of straight to MUST NOT. A new algorithm is expected to enter with SHOULD rather than MUST. Any algorithm in the IANA registry that this document does not mention MAY be implemented, and an algorithm is called MAY only when it has been downgraded.

Rows marked (IoT) apply to Internet of Things devices and to server-side implementations, including general-purpose VPN gateways, that must interoperate with them.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of traffic signs. Some say you must do something, some say you should, and some say never. A few say that a rule will probably get stricter later.

sections.title: Encryption, PRF and Integrity Algorithms
sections.content:
For encryption, ENCR_AES_CBC is raised to MUST for 128-bit and 256-bit keys, and 192-bit keys stay at MAY. It is the only algorithm that is mandatory in both RFC 4307 and this document, which keeps new and old implementations interoperable. ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 and ENCR_AES_GCM_16 are SHOULD, and both are Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithms. ENCR_AES_CCM_8 is SHOULD for 128-bit keys, for interoperability with IoT. ENCR_3DES drops from MUST- to MAY, and ENCR_DES and ENCR_NULL are MUST NOT. DES can be brute-forced with off-the-shelf hardware.

For the pseudorandom function (PRF), PRF_HMAC_SHA2_256 is MUST and PRF_HMAC_SHA2_512 is SHOULD+. PRF_HMAC_SHA1 is downgraded to MUST- because attacks on SHA1 are increasing. PRF_HMAC_MD5 is MUST NOT. PRF_AES128_XCBC is SHOULD for IoT.

Integrity algorithms are used only with non-AEAD encryption. AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 is MUST and AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 is SHOULD. AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96 is MUST-. AUTH_AES_XCBC_96 is SHOULD for IoT. AUTH_HMAC_MD5_96, AUTH_DES_MAC and AUTH_KPDK_MD5 are MUST NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a list of locks and scramblers. A few trusty ones are required, newer ones are recommended, and ones that thieves can pick easily are banned.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Groups
sections.content:
The Diffie-Hellman exchange provides the keys for the session, so the RFC says it is critical to enforce a secure one. An attacker who can recover the private numbers and the matching public values can compute the secret and decrypt the exchange and the IPsec SA created inside it. Unlike an attack on authentication, this can be done off-line on a recorded communication, years later.

Group 14, the 2048-bit MODP group, rises to MUST. Group 19, the 256-bit random ECP group, is SHOULD. Group 5 (1536-bit) and group 2 (1024-bit) become SHOULD NOT, because their security margin is too narrow, and group 2 is expected to become MUST NOT in the near future. Group 1 (768-bit) is MUST NOT, since it can be broken within hours using cheap off-the-shelf hardware.

Groups 22, 23 and 24 use prime order subgroups that are not safe primes, and their seeds have not been publicly released. Group 22 is MUST NOT, and groups 23 and 24 are SHOULD NOT. When groups 23 or 24 are used, the checks in the first bullet of Section 2.2 of RFC 6989 MUST be done.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people agree on a secret by mixing paint colors in public. If the paint pot is too small, a snoop can guess the mix, so this list bans small pots.

sections.title: Authentication Methods and Signatures
sections.content:
Authentication in IKEv2 may involve verifying signatures, either to validate a certificate or to check the signature on the AUTH value. Certificate validation rules are out of scope and left to the PKIX community.

Of the authentication methods, RSA Digital Signature (1) and Shared Key Message Integrity Code (2) are MUST. DSS Digital Signature (3) is SHOULD NOT, because its signatures are bound to SHA-1 and have the same security level as 1024-bit RSA. The three ECDSA methods (9, 10, 11) and the generic Digital Signature method (14) are SHOULD. The generic method from RFC 7427 is expected to be promoted, since it gives hash, signature format and algorithm agility.

For RSA keys, length 2048 is MUST, 3072 and 4096 are SHOULD, lengths from 2049 to 4095 are MAY, and anything under 2048 is SHOULD NOT. This is a change to what RFC 7296 says about 1024-bit keys. Smaller keys are kept at SHOULD NOT instead of MUST NOT because these signatures only matter in real time and need no future protection.

When the Digital Signature method is used, the hash function SHA2-256 is MUST, SHA2-512 is SHOULD, SHA2-384 is MAY and SHA1 is MUST NOT. With RSA, RSASSA-PSS MUST be supported and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1.5 MAY be.
sections.plainLanguage: Proving who you are with a signature only works if the pen cannot be forged. Short keys are like easily copied signatures, so the RFC asks for longer ones.

sections.title: Algorithms for the Internet of Things
sections.content:
Some algorithms are marked for IoT because constrained devices have so little memory and CPU power that they can only afford one set of algorithms. For instance, a device may use AES_XCBC as its integrity algorithm so it does not need to implement SHA.

Many such devices already have hardware for AES-CCM, used for link-level security in IEEE Std 802.15.4. They often cannot use AES-CBC, because that hardware may lack the AES decryption it needs. So AES-CCM is preferred even though it requires AEAD support.

Transfer rates are low, in the order of tens of kbit/s, and every bit sent costs battery life. That is why the 8-octet integrity check value is recommended over the 16-octet one. Because IoT devices vary, the RFC does not define one mandatory IoT profile and only points out commonly used algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets have small brains and small batteries. They get their own shorter list of tools, so they do not run out of power.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security depends on the strength of the algorithms, the strength of the keys and the engineering of the protocol around them. The Diffie-Hellman group is the parameter to choose most conservatively. Anyone who captures all IKE and ESP traffic and, even years later, can break the selected group can get the symmetric keys that encrypt all the ESP traffic. But an extremely large group puts heavy load on the device, especially a large VPN gateway or a constrained IoT device.

Algorithms marked MUST or SHOULD are not known to be broken now, and research suggests they will likely stay secure for the foreseeable future. The RFC says this is not necessarily forever, and that new revisions are expected from time to time.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thief records your secret messages today and cracks the lock in ten years, they can read everything. So the first lock must be very strong.

sections.title: IANA Registry Clean-up
sections.content:
The document makes a small clean-up in the Transform Type 1 (Encryption Algorithm) registry of the IKEv2 Parameters. Names there did not follow one pattern, so IANA renamed six entries. The AES-GCM entries with 8, 12 and 16 octet ICVs became ENCR_AES_GCM_8, ENCR_AES_GCM_12 and ENCR_AES_GCM_16. The Camellia CCM entries became ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM_8, ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM_12 and ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM_16.

IANA also added this RFC as a reference for the ENCR_AES_GCM and ENCR_CAMELLIA_CCM entries, while keeping the existing references.
sections.plainLanguage: It tidies the labels in a big catalog so they all look alike and are easier to find.
